executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is the consolidation of Texas as a defining battleground for American political power and cultural identity. The Economist's 'Pax Texana' newsletter and the breaking news out of Texas's primary runoffs tell a unified story: Ken Paxton's upset defeat of incumbent Senator John Cornyn signals a hard-right populist takeover of Texas Republican politics, effectively ending the era of establishment GOP dominance in the state that has been a cornerstone of national conservative strategy. This matters because Texas is not a peripheral story — it is the test case for whether Trumpian political energy can permanently displace traditional Republican institutionalism at the state level, with direct implications for the 2026 Senate map and beyond. The Economist's framing of 'Pax Texana' likely anticipates exactly this shift: a Texas that increasingly sets the terms for national Republican identity rather than simply reflecting it. With no longform analysis available today to contextualize the electoral results more deeply, the breaking news and newsletter signals alone are sufficient to establish this as the day's most consequential story.

items.headline: Iran and the Forever War Trap: In Trying to Avoid a Quagmire, America Found a Dead End
items.blurb: In Iran, the Trump administration fell "prey to the short-war fallacy, focusing inordinately on the power of its means while losing sight of how to achieve its ends." Great powers tend to assume that "moving fast with tremendous force will incapacitate adversaries and achieve swift success on the battlefield," but "wars do not often end so easily." Today, the United States' gambit in Iran "may not turn out to be a long war, but it has already failed as a short war."

newsletters.title: Ground beef, asparagus and tofu, stir-fried in a flash

items.headline: Beef, Asparagus and Tofu Stir-Fry
items.blurb: Adding crumbled firm tofu along with the ground beef makes the dish both lighter and more economical, and I love the way the tofu stays a little soft while the meat browns in spots. Then Kay adds the asparagus toward the end to preserve its bright color and crisp-tender texture.

items.headline: Chile Chicken and Bean Guisado
items.blurb: Inspired by the flavors of Mexican chorizo, Kristina Felix's white bean and chicken stew gets seasoned with tomatoes, vinegar, cinnamon and ancho chile powder, which adds a characteristically fruity-smoky depth. It's a savory and substantial one-pot meal that can be on the table in about half an hour.

items.headline: Spicy Sardine Pasta With Leeks and Lemon
items.blurb: Tinned fish doesn't need much help to become a meal: Just open the top and grab a hunk of bread. But for something a little more satisfying, Ashley Lonsdale mashes canned sardines into a pan of sautéed garlic and leeks for sweetness, with chiles for heat and capers for pizazz, then tosses it all with spaghetti. And if sardines aren't your thing, the recipe works just as well with canned tuna, anchovies or salmon.

items.headline: Spicy Shrimp Salad With Mint
items.blurb: You can sear the paprika- and garlic-seasoned shrimp for this classic Mark Bittman recipe under the broiler, on the stovetop or on the grill, as long as you let the pink crustaceans get a little singed at their edges. Then serve them over an arugula and mint salad for a summery dish that's excellent all year-round.

items.headline: Charred Corn and Pickled Jalapeño Potato Salad
items.blurb: This vibrant potato salad might be slightly too involved for this week, but I've got the recipe bookmarked for the weekend. Then I'll have time to follow Sue Li's genius directions for slathering mayonnaise on the corn before searing it in a skillet, which adds a layer of smokiness while keeping the kernels sweet and juicy. With soft potatoes and pickled jalapeños, the salad is a zippy accompaniment for whatever else you've got on the table.

items.headline: Ice Cream With Olive Oil and Dates
items.blurb: Just because I'm busy doesn't mean I'm skipping dessert. My go-to for harried moments is Ali Slagle's no-cook recipe, which turns a pint of ice cream into a delightfully sweet-savory way to end the day.

items.headline: Mina Kimes spells out success
items.blurb: For my money, the smartest on-air talent in sports media is ESPN's Mina Kimes. Yale alum, Emmy-winning NFL analyst, polymath podcaster, reigning "Celebrity Jeopardy" champion and — this week — first-time host of the Scripps National Spelling Bee (ION, 8 p.m. ET tonight for the tape-delayed semis and 8 p.m. ET tomorrow for the live final). Ahead of her Bee debut, Kimes talked with my colleague Jayna Bardahl in a fascinating, wide-ranging interview that covered everything from Bee prep to the NFL player who would make the best Bee participant (spoiler: M-Y-L-E-S G-A-R-R-E-T-T).

items.blurb: I lived in NYC in 1999, the last time the Knicks made the NBA Finals. The city gets a surge of energy around the team's success like no other sports result. There is real cognitive dissonance between the managerial doldrums of the past three decades and this. How did it happen?

items.headline: MIT Technology Review Narrated: what's next for IVF
items.blurb: IVF has brought millions of babies into the world over the last four decades. But the process can still be slow, painful, and expensive—and far from guaranteed to work. Now, a wave of new technologies aims to change that. Researchers are using AI to identify promising sperm and embryos, developing robotic systems that could automate parts of the IVF process, and even exploring controversial genetic editing techniques designed to prevent inherited disease. The technologies could make IVF more effective and accessible. But they're also raising difficult ethical questions about how far reproductive medicine should go.

items.headline: Only sort of wrong about Clemson?
items.blurb: A year ago at this time, Dabo Swinney's Clemson revival appeared to be well within reach. After nearly a half-decade of the Tigers no longer looking like the two-time champs of the 2010s, they had a roster that sure looked loaded, complete with veteran quarterback Cade Klubnik and likely first-round defensive tackle Peter Woods. This week, our draft expert Dane Brugler looked back at his top-50 rankings from last summer. At the time, he led with Woods (who ended up going No. 29 to the Chiefs) and had three other eventually drafted Tigers in his top 30.

newsletters.title: The US in Brief: Pax Texana

items.headline: Pax Texana: Ken Paxton wins Senate primary
items.blurb: Ken Paxton, Texas's scandal-ridden attorney-general, won a primary to become the Republican nominee for a seat in the Senate. He trounced John Cornyn, the four-term incumbent. That's another win for Donald Trump, who gave Mr Paxton a late endorsement; the president has backed candidates to unseat lawmakers who have crossed him, and many have won. But no one will cheer louder than the Democrats. They believe that James Talarico, a cool-headed seminarian, has a better chance of winning against Mr Paxton in the midterm elections in November than he would have had against Mr Cornyn.

items.headline: Texas Democratic run-offs settled after Republican redistricting
items.blurb: Run-offs also settled some bitter primary contests between Democrats after Republicans redrew Texas's congressional map last year. Johnny Garcia, a moderate backed by Washington Democrats, beat a sex therapist with extreme views on Zionism in a redrawn district that is now expected to go Republican. Meanwhile, Christian Menefee, a 38-year-old congressman, defeated Al Green, 78, a congressman for more than two decades, after Republican gerrymandering forced them to vie for the same Houston seat.

items.headline: South Carolina Senate rejects map eliminating majority-black district; Alabama map blocked
items.blurb: South Carolina's Republican-controlled Senate rejected a congressional map that would eliminate a majority-black district. The measure, backed by Mr Trump and passed by the state's lower house, would have required new primary elections. Early voting is already under way. Separately, a federal court blocked Alabama from using a redrawn map that it found discriminatory against black voters. Republicans had also implemented it too late, it ruled.

items.headline: Joe Biden sues Justice Department over memoir ghostwriter conversations
items.blurb: Joe Biden sued the Justice Department in a bid to stop the release of conversations between him and the ghostwriter of his memoir. They were evidence in an investigation of the former president's handling of classified documents. In 2024, during Mr Biden's presidency, the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think-tank, filed a Freedom of Information Act request for the materials. The Justice Department said no. Under Mr Trump it has changed its mind.

items.headline: Minneapolis police chief Brian O'Hara resigns amid investigation
items.blurb: Minneapolis's police chief, Brian O'Hara, resigned after he was accused of interfering with an internal investigation of allegations that he had had sexual relationships with city workers. A report found he had probably deleted a contact from his phone, though it discovered no evidence of relationships. Mr O'Hara began leading the police department in 2022, while it was reeling from an officer's murder of George Floyd in 2020. He was highly critical of the recent federal immigration crackdown in the city.

On the emergency management front, authorities in Southern California lifted evacuation orders after a chemical tank that had prompted the precautionary measures cooled sufficiently to no longer pose a threat to nearby residents [1]. No injuries were reported in connection with the incident.
